title: PAGASA iHeatMap & Heat Safety

competencies.text: Describe how PAGASA iHEAT maps help Filipinos.

days.title: PAGASA and the Heat Index
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will describe how PAGASA's heat index maps (iHeatMap) help Filipinos prepare for and stay safe from extreme heat.

🌤️ PAGASA

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration is the national weather agency under the Department of Science and Technology (DOST). It forecasts weather, monitors tropical cyclones, issues rainfall and heat advisories, tracks El Niño and La Niña, and provides climate data.

🌡️ What Is the Heat Index?

The heat index is the "feels-like" temperature. It combines air temperature and relative humidity. Our bodies cool down when sweat evaporates. When the air is humid, sweat evaporates slowly, so we feel hotter than the thermometer shows. For example, an air temperature of 33 °C with high humidity can feel like 42 °C or more.

Heat indexCategoryPossible effects
27–32 °CCautionFatigue with long exposure and activity
33–41 °CExtreme CautionHeat cramps and heat exhaustion possible
42–51 °CDangerHeat cramps and exhaustion likely; heat stroke probable with continued exposure
52 °C and aboveExtreme DangerHeat stroke likely

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: What two factors does the heat index combine?

choices.label: Air temperature and humidity
Wind speed and amount of rainfall
Air pressure and cloud cover
Sea level and ocean temperature

scenario.explanation: The heat index uses temperature and humidity to estimate how hot it feels to the body.

scenario.text: Why does humid air make you feel hotter?

choices.label: Sweat evaporates slowly, so cooling slows
Humid air contains more heat from the Sun
Water vapor burns the skin when it is hot
Humid air makes the heart beat very slowly

scenario.explanation: Evaporating sweat removes heat. In humid air, evaporation slows, so the body cannot cool itself as well.

scenario.text: A heat index of 45 °C falls in which category?

choices.label: Danger
Caution
Extreme Caution
Normal

scenario.explanation: 42–51 °C is the Danger category, where heat exhaustion is likely and heat stroke is probable with continued exposure.

days.title: Reading the iHeatMap
days.content:
🗺️ iHeatMap

In 2025, PAGASA launched the Interactive Heat Index Mapping and Prediction (iHeatMap) platform on its website. (Your curriculum calls these "iHEAT maps.") It gives nationwide, real-time heat index data.

  • High-resolution, gridded map — shows the heat index across the whole country, not just at weather stations.
  • Color-coded alerts — yellow (Caution), yellow-orange (Extreme Caution), red-orange (Danger), red (Extreme Danger).
  • Hourly updates and forecasts — shows when the hottest hours will be.
  • Location search — check your own city or municipality.
  • Summary — recent days and short-range forecast by region and station.

🏙️ Urban Heat Islands

Cities are often hotter than nearby rural areas because concrete and asphalt absorb heat by day and release it at night, there are fewer trees, and vehicles and aircons add heat. This is the urban heat island effect — visible on detailed heat maps.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: It shows real-time and forecast heat index.

match.right: Feels-like temperature from heat and humidity
Heat exhaustion likely; heat stroke probable

match.why: Move to shade and drink water.

match.right: Very high body temperature, confusion, may stop sweating

days.title: Using Heat Information to Stay Safe
days.content:
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Who Uses Heat Maps?

UserDecision
FamiliesPlan errands for cooler morning or late-afternoon hours; check on elderly relatives and young children
SchoolsMove outdoor activities, adjust class schedules, ensure drinking water and ventilation
Outdoor workers and farmersStart work early, take shade breaks, drink water regularly
LGUs and health officesIssue advisories, open cooling centers, prepare health workers for heat illness cases

🛟 First Aid

  • Heat exhaustion: move to a cool, shaded place, loosen clothing, sip water, apply cool, wet cloths.
  • Heat stroke (confusion, very hot skin, fainting): call for emergency help immediately and cool the person quickly while waiting.

Avoid relying on drinks like coffee, softdrinks or alcohol for hydration in extreme heat; water is best.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Use heat information to make decisions. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: The iHeatMap shows a heat index of 45 °C in your city this afternoon. What should you do?

choices.label: Stay in shade at peak hours and drink water
Play basketball outdoors at noon to build tolerance
Drink softdrinks instead of water to stay cool
Wear thick dark clothes to block the sunlight

scenario.explanation: 45 °C is in the Danger range. Avoiding peak-hour sun and staying hydrated reduces the risk of heat illness.

scenario.text: A principal sees a forecast heat index of 43 °C for tomorrow. What is the BEST action?

choices.label: Move outdoor events to early morning or indoors
Hold the outdoor program at noon exactly as planned
Ask students to bring less water to school
Close all classroom windows to keep heat out

scenario.explanation: In the Danger range, rescheduling outdoor activities to cooler times or indoor spaces protects students.

scenario.text: A construction worker becomes confused and stops sweating after hours in the sun. What should co-workers do?

choices.label: Call for help and cool him down at once
Let him keep working until his shift ends
Give him strong coffee to wake him up
Wait for him to feel better on his own

scenario.explanation: Confusion and lack of sweating suggest heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency requiring rapid cooling and medical care.

scenario.text: A barangay wants to reduce its urban heat island effect. Which plan is MOST effective?

choices.label: Plant shade trees; use light-colored roofs
Pave all of the open spaces with dark asphalt
Cut down trees to let the wind through
Add more parking lots near the plaza

scenario.explanation: Trees provide shade and cooling; light roofs reflect sunlight — both lower urban temperatures.

scenario.text: A farmer sees on the iHeatMap forecast that Wednesday will reach Danger level. How should he plan his work?

choices.label: Work early in the day; rest at midday
Work only between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. that day
Skip drinking water so he can work longer
Plan to work in the open field all day long

scenario.explanation: Planning heavy work for cooler hours and resting at midday reduces heat stress.

days.title: Heat, Climate Change and Community Action
days.content:
📈 A Warming Trend

As the climate warms, the Philippines is experiencing more days with Danger-level heat index, especially during the dry season and El Niño years. In recent years, some schools shifted to shorter or alternative class schedules on extremely hot days.

🌳 Community Adaptation

  • Plant and protect trees in streets, schools and plazas.
  • Use reflective roofing and good ventilation in classrooms and houses.
  • Set up cooling and hydration stations during heat events.
  • Use PAGASA heat forecasts in barangay and school DRRM plans.

🧠 Why Data Matters

Heat illness is preventable. Real-time, location-specific information turns a vague warning ("It's hot") into specific actions ("Avoid outdoor work from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. in this barangay today"). That is how science-based tools like the iHeatMap save lives.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

choices.label: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
Philippine Agency for Global Atmospheric, Geological and Aeronautical Studies
Philippine Association of Geologists and Atmospheric Scientists
Public Advisory Group on Atmospheric Safety and Alerts

escape.explanation: PAGASA is the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration under DOST.

escape.text: What does the heat index measure?

choices.label: How hot it feels to the human body
The temperature of the ground surface
The amount of sunlight in one hour
The speed of hot winds from the sea

escape.explanation: It is the apparent, feels-like temperature from heat and humidity combined.

escape.text: Which heat index range is classified as DANGER?

choices.label: 52 °C and above

escape.explanation: 42–51 °C is Danger; 52 °C and above is Extreme Danger.

escape.text: What should you do FIRST for someone with signs of heat stroke?

choices.label: Call for help and cool them down
Give them hot soup to restore their energy
Let them sleep it off in the sun
Make them run to sweat out the heat

escape.explanation: Heat stroke is life-threatening. Get medical help and cool the person immediately.

escape.text: What is the urban heat island effect?

choices.label: Cities hotter than their surroundings
Islands becoming colder during typhoons
Heat from volcanoes warming coastal cities
Forests becoming hotter than nearby towns

escape.explanation: Concrete, asphalt, fewer trees and waste heat make cities warmer than rural areas.

escape.text: How can the iHeatMap help an LGU?

choices.label: It shows where and when to warn people
It predicts earthquakes all over the region
It measures the depth of local rivers
It controls the weather over the town

escape.explanation: Location-specific, hourly heat data helps LGUs target advisories, cooling centers and health response.
